title: The yogis' earrings
hook: the yogis offer Nanak their earrings, bag and patched coat; he names what he'd wear instead

segments.voice: Yesterday the yogis asked why Nanak left home, and he said he went searching for the Gurmukhs, a trader in truth. Your line was seeking the good. What good thing did you pass on? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-six.

A ring through the ear is hard to take off. The yogis Nanak met wore earrings as a mark of their order, and tradition says the ring marked an initiation, a road a person had chosen for good. Add a shoulder bag and a coat stitched together from patches, and the look was unmistakable. In the Sidh Gosht they make Nanak an offer. Take on our look, our earrings, our bag, our patched coat. Join us. Today: the yogis' earrings, and what he'd wear instead.
screen: `A RING THAT DOESN'T COME OFF.` → `EARRINGS, BAG, PATCHED COAT.` → `JOIN US, THEY SAY.`

segments.voice: It's a generous offer, and it's made with pride: our path is the best of the yogic paths, the yogis say, in paraphrase. Nanak doesn't mock the earrings. He takes each piece and moves it inside. Here's his answer, in paraphrase. Let the Word, the shabad, be the earring, worn within, never taken out. Clear away ego and the grip of mine. Let go of lust, anger and pride, and through the Guru's Word, real understanding comes. And for the patched coat and the bag: see the Lord filling everything, everywhere. The One, Nanak says, carries a person across. Look at what he kept. He kept the idea of the earring: something worn always, a mark of who you belong to, a sign you aren't going back. He just put it where nobody can see it. The yogi's ring is in the ear; Nanak's is in what the ear keeps hearing. The coat is the same. The yogi's coat is made of scraps sewn together. Nanak's is the whole world, with the One stitched through every piece of it. You may remember an echo of this from the Japji, where he gave the yogis earrings of contentment. Here, in the Sidh Gosht, the earring is the Word itself. Now think about what an earring does all day. You forget it's there. Then you catch it in a mirror, or it brushes your neck when you turn your head, and you remember. That's one way to picture what the stanza asks of the Word: a line of Gurbani that keeps catching the light through an ordinary day, bringing you back. That's the line for today. The word as earring.
screen: `OUR PATH IS BEST, THE YOGIS SAY.` · `THE WORD IS THE EARRING, WITHIN.` · `THE COAT: THE ONE IN EVERYTHING.` · `IT CATCHES THE LIGHT ALL DAY.` · then, large: `THE WORD AS EARRING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wear an inner ornament. Settle into the breath. Choose one short line you've met on this path, a line of Gurbani or just a word, Waheguru, or today's line itself. Imagine fastening it in place, the way you'd put on an earring in the morning, once and carefully. Then let it go quiet. Every few breaths, let it catch the light again: the line, there, still in place. If your mind wanders, that's fine; an earring is easy to forget. Each time you notice, you've found it again. If you pray, the line you chose can be the prayer, worn quietly. The bell holds the time.
The yogis' earrings. Their offer of earrings, bag and patched coat, and Nanak's answer: let the Word be the earring, and the One in everything be the coat. Today's word.
Your line: the word as earring. Today, each time you catch your reflection, in a mirror, a window or a phone screen, let your line catch the light. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs do not take on the yogis' earrings or patched coat; the Sidh Gosht's answer is read as moving those outward marks inward, and some keep a line of Gurbani in mind through the day as a way of wearing the Word.

original.note: mundra: the yogi's earring, which Nanak's answer turns into the Word worn within.

trapdoor: what you thought: the earrings are just yogis' jewelry.
what it means: Nanak keeps the earring and makes it the Word, worn inside.
what a scholar hears: the Sidh Gosht reworks the Nath yogis' insignia one by one, as the Japji's earrings of contentment did.
